newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French markets weak on talk of EU pact delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French markets weak on talk of EU pact delay.

text.p: French markets weakened sharply on Monday as investors reacted to the Socialist-led government's calls for a "period of reflection" on a pact limiting budget deficits of countries that join a single European currency.

Analysts said the demand, which amounted to a delay in the timetable for ratification of the so-called stability pact, added more uncertainty to the creation of the euro, but did not spell the end of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The Paris Bourse, which was trading lower before the comments, slid to 2.2 percent down but then bounced off the bottom and stabilised around 2,671, off nearly 1.8 percent.
The franc fell by more than half a centime to 3.3825 per mark, but held above last week's low of 3.3860 set after the combined left swept to power in a June 1 election upset.

The new French government, headed by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, set down several conditions during his election campaign for going ahead with EMU, including the participation of Italy and the creation of an economic government to counterbalance the power of a future independent European central bank.

However, he said the conditions, along with his reservations about the stability pact, should serve as a basis for discussion and that France remains committed to launching the single currency on time.

"It would appear from this that the Socialist government is maybe a little more serious ultimately than some had taken them to be. Jospin wants to maintain his credibility," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais.

French bond futures fell from their earlier highs but clung to positive ground. The yield spread between German and French ten year bonds, a gauge of investor risk assessment, narrowed to minus four basis points from minus nine on Friday.
"I don't think people are so much buying Germany. (German bonds) are outperforming as they're not being sold as much as France," Sonja Gibbs, bond analyst at Nomura International said.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn called on Monday for a period of reflection before agreeing to the stability pact. But he said France was not seeking to renegotiate the pact and was totally committed to a timely EMU start in 1999.

Diplomats said Strauss-Kahn told European Union ministers in Luxembourg that Jospin wanted to inform the National Assembly about the pact on June 19, two days after an EU summit was supposed to have approved the agreement in Amsterdam.
The new French cabinet was planning a special meeting this Thursday to discuss policy priorities and Jospin is expected to present the programme on June 19.

"The risk is more that the market sees a real conflict between France and Germany - some of the comments coming out from (German finance minister Theo) Waigel sound unfriendly - even though in the longer run it does not mean an end to EMU if there's no stability pact in Amsterdam," Gibbs said.

Economists said the added uncertainty in markets could cause volatility until it was clear a compromise could be reached on the pact, which Bonn sees as crucial to maintaining a credible euro currency.
"Until they kiss and make up, we could see the franc go up and down," said Steven Englander, economist at Smith Barney.
